messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marco

Marco was twenty-two when he accidentally drove the nail gun through his coworker's leg. It was a Tuesday morning in April, unremarkable except for what happened in the span of three seconds. They were framing a residential addition in Albuquerque, and Marco had been running the gun along the top plate, moving fast because the foreman was pushing to stay on schedule. His coworker, Javier, had stepped into the space where Marco was working—Marco didn't see him, or rather, Marco's mind didn't register him until the sound came: not the usual pneumatic pop of the gun, but a different sound, wet and wrong, followed by Javier's scream. The nail had gone through the meat of his thigh, and for a moment Marco couldn't move. He could smell the heat from the compressor, the acrid metallic tang of the nail gun's exhaust, the sharp copper scent of blood. Javier was on the ground, and Marco was standing above him holding the gun, and everyone was shouting. Javier spent two weeks in the hospital. He recovered, mostly. But Marco did not.

In the months that followed, Marco came to believe that he was fundamentally unreliable—not just careless, but broken in some essential way. His own body had betrayed both him and Javier. His hands, which he had always trusted to do their work, had become instruments of harm. He couldn't look at them without feeling a surge of disgust and dread. What frightened him most was the thought that he might do something like that again, that some part of him was incapable of the basic attention required to keep other people safe. He had not done enough to stop what happened; he had been careless, inattentive, and now he was a person who hurt people. This conviction—that he was unrecognizable to himself, that the careful, responsible person he'd believed he was had never existed—drove him to withdraw from almost everything. He stopped going to job sites. He stopped answering calls from his crew. He told his mother he was sick, and after a while, the lies became easier than the truth. He couldn't bear the thought of being around people who might depend on him, people he might accidentally harm. Staying home felt like the only ethical choice.

But staying home meant avoiding anything that could trigger the memory, which meant avoiding almost everything. He couldn't watch certain movies, couldn't listen to certain songs, couldn't be in hardware stores or anywhere near pneumatic tools. He started keeping a list—not written down, but catalogued in his mind—of all the things that felt dangerous. Loud noises made him flinch. The smell of metal or oil could send him spiraling. He began to structure his days around avoidance: he would only leave the house to buy groceries at a specific store, at a specific time, when he knew it would be quiet. He avoided anniversaries of the accident with ritualistic precision, calling in sick on that date every month, though no one had asked him to. He overanalyzed the event constantly, replaying those three seconds again and again, trying to find the moment where he could have prevented it, the split-second decision he could have unmade. If only he'd been standing two feet to the left. If only he'd looked over his shoulder. If only, if only. But the overanalysis never brought resolution—it only deepened his conviction that he was someone who couldn't be trusted.

The memory itself had taken on a strange quality. When it surfaced—and it surfaced constantly, without warning, forcing its way into his mind at odd moments—it felt like it was happening to someone else. He could see himself holding the gun, could see Javier falling, but the person in that memory didn't feel like him. It was as though he were watching a video of a stranger committing an unforgivable act. Yet the memory was also viscerally present: he could smell the compressor heat, the blood, the metal. His body would react before his mind could catch up—his heart would race, his hands would shake, sweat would break out on his palms. The physical reactivity was immediate and overwhelming, a betrayal by the very body he had come to distrust. And because the memory was so intrusive, so uncontrollable, he found himself increasingly confined to the few places where he felt safe: his bedroom, his mother's kitchen, the backyard where he could see all approaches. Anywhere else felt dangerous, not because of any logical threat, but because the memory could ambush him there, and he couldn't predict or control what his body might do in response.

The silence was the worst part. When things were quiet—when there were no external stimuli to distract him—the memory was most likely to surface. He had come to believe that unusual silence meant something dangerous was about to happen, that the quiet itself was a warning. He started playing music constantly, leaving the television on even when he wasn't watching it, anything to fill the void where the memory might emerge. His mother found him one afternoon sitting in the dark with the radio on, unable to articulate why he couldn't turn it off. He was trapped in a cycle he couldn't name: his conviction that he was untrustworthy made him avoid situations where he might be tested; his avoidance meant he never had the chance to disconfirm that belief. The memory remained intrusive and unprocessed, triggering the physical fear responses that kept him confined to his safe zones, which in turn left him alone with the silence and the smell-memories and the grinding, endless loop of self-recrimination. He had been out of work for eight months when he finally called a therapist. He was terrified that talking about it would make it worse, but he was more terrified of spending the rest of his life imprisoned in four rooms, waiting for the memory to strike.
